newsitem.title: FINLAND: FIM HAS NO SECRET NARROWER BAND IN ERM - HAMALAINEN.
newsitem.headline: FIM HAS NO SECRET NARROWER BAND IN ERM - HAMALAINEN.

text.p: The markka will not be forced into any secretly pre-defined narrower band inside the broad fluctuation limits of Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism, Bank of Finland governor Sirkka Hamalainen said on Saturday.
"The fluctuation bands are plus-minus 15 percent," Hamalainen told a news conference after Finland decided to peg the markka to ERM at a central parity rate of 3.04 per mark.
"It is likely that the markka's external value against ERM currencies will remain quite stable," the central bank said in a statement.
But the definition of stability was open, Hamalainen said.

"It is quite clear that the definition of stability will not be plus-minus 15 (percent), but (stability) has not been defined anywhere, and it is quite obvious that it is not 2-1/4 (percent up or down)," she said. "There does not exist any narrower fluctuation range (than 15 percent)," she added.
Since the fluctuation bands are so wide, there would be "plenty of room to move from the point of view of speculation," Hamalainen said.
"But it is also quite clear that the ... limits cannot be used very easily in practice because if we come close to the limits it will create a speculative situation," she said.
"In such a situation the Bank of Finland would be obliged to curb exchange rate fluctuations largely by effecting changes in short-term interest rates," the central bank's statement said.
"Currency buying and selling can only temporarily restrain currency market pressure," it added.

Hamalainen said participation in ERM would include, in principle, the possibility of intervention by other countries belonging to the mechanism. "But these are exceptions and will only come near the limits of the fluctuation bands," she said.
Keeping its own currency within the set limits was primarily the task of each central bank.
"If the exchange rate comes under pressure we must react, as a last resort by means of monetary policy," Hamalainen said.
Thanks to the economic stability achieved in recent years and the favourable outlook, such speculative pressures were not on the horizon, she said.
"The exchange rate has been very stable ... Since autumn 1994 it has fluctuated relatively little," Hamalainen said.
Against the German mark, the markka has moved between 2.95 and 3.17 markka since the end of 1994, the Bank of Finland statement said.
"The firm economic policy has meant that confidence in the exchange rate has increased, this has come to light very clearly in the narrowing of the interest rate differential," Hamalainen said.
Finnish short-term interest rates are currently at the level of Germany, and the gap in long-term rates over Bunds is less than half a percentage point, she noted.
"According to forecasts Finnish economic performance should continue on a favourable path over the coming years (and) wage developments should remain moderate," the statement said.
"Conditions for the attainment of the price stability objective are favourable," it added.
Hamalainen said everything indicated that the agreed central parity exchange rate was "well in rhyme with our economic trend ... and economic policy."

The central parity rate was "quite well in line with the kind of stability that has been created ... This means the continuation of exactly the same kind of monetary policy (as before the ERM link) ... and aiming at the same kind of inflation and cost trends as until now," she said.
"The core trends in our economic policy remain completely unchanged and so the stability of the exchange rate should be the same from here onwards too," Hamalainen added.

It had become topical to link the markka to ERM because of apparently increasing certainty that the planned third stage of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would start on schedule in January 1999, the Bank of Finland said.
"Commencement of stage three of EMU at the beginning of 1999 is viewed as ever more certain also in the international financial and foreign exchange markets," it said.
"The view that this is the case has recently strengthened very clearly," Hamalainen echoed.
--Peter Starck, Helsinki Newsroom +358 - 0 - 680 50 245
